messages.subject: Distance Sampling Workshop, August 2012, University St. Andrews
messages.subject_clean: Distance Sampling Workshop, August 2012, University St. Andrews
messages.body_plain:
The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling  (CRE=
EM) is hosting three linked workshops in the summer of 2012 in our purpos=
e-built facilities at the University of St Andrews, Scotland. The aim of =
these workshops is to train participants in the latest methods for design=
 and analysis of distance sampling surveys, including line and point tran=
sects. The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the field, usin=
g industry-standard software.

The first workshop (21-24 August) will run at an introductory level, and =
will focus on "conventional" distance sampling methods, as described in t=
he standard reference book "Introduction to Distance Sampling." The works=
hop will be a blend of theory and practice and participants will learn ho=
w to use the program "Distance." Participants will gain a solid grounding=
 in both survey design and methods of analysis for distance sampling surv=
eys.  Note that we have moved the 'automated survey design' topic out of =
the advanced workshop into the introductory workshop.=20=20

The advanced distance sampling workshop (27-30 August) will include advan=
ced treatment of: incorporating covariates in detection function modellin=
g, analyses in which detectability on the transect line is not assumed to=
 be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem) and spatial (or  density surface=
) modelling. The aim of this workshop is to bring participants up to date=
 with the latest developments in distance sampling methods and software. =
It is also an opportunity for those actively engaged in the design, analy=
sis and execution of distance sampling surveys to discuss common issues a=
nd problems, and set future research directions. The workshop will be a c=
ombination of lectures and computer sessions, with considerable time for =
discussion.=20=20

In addition, this year we are running a one-day introduction to density e=
stimation from passive acoustic data (25 August).  Passive acoustic monit=
oring is often used to obtain indices of relative abundance, such as numb=
er of detections per unit time. However, for many applications, the quant=
ity we really want to estimate is absolute population abundance (i.e., th=
e number of animals in the population) or density (number of animals per =
unit area). This day-long tutorial will give an insight into methods to a=
chieve this.

For all workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data se=
ts, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.  Comp=
uter sessions take place in our modern computer classroom (attached to th=
e seminar room); participants can use our computers or bring their own la=
ptops.=20=20

Additional details regarding the workshop can be found at our website htt=
p://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/distance2012/workshop_overv= <http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/distance2012/workshop_overv=>
iew.html

messages.subject: Interaction term
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I was wondering if you can include an interaction term as a predictor with =
the density surface modeling in Distance 6.1? The "help" index has 2 sugges=
tions--either create a new field and multiply the predictor values together=
 beforehand or use a:b or a*b when specifying the model formula.  I would l=
ike to use the latter suggestion so I have more options for plotting the te=
rms with the response variable either in Distance or R.  However, I have tr=
ied including various combinations of my 2 interaction terms, such as ~s(a*=
b), ~s(a,b), ~s(a:b), ~s(a)*(b) without much luck. I either get an error me=
ssage (ie-model has repeated 1-d smooths of same variable) or it runs with =
no errors, but the resulting surface plots don't make biological sense. One=
 term is linear and the other is non-parametric--this could be part of the =
problem?  I'm hoping there is a way to do this besides separating my data i=
nto 2 groups and analyzing them separately. Thanks so much for any suggesti=
ons!

Jennifer Timmer

--

messages.subject: Re: maximum observations in MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Kristine:

Because the MCDS engine in Distance is compiled FORTRAN code, the
dimensions of various arrays is limited to 100,000.  In the mists of
time, I recall another user who exceeded this number of observations.  I
will check with the development team whether a compiled version with
larger dimensions might still exist.

Depending upon what you are trying to accomplish with MCDS, you might
see whether MRDS running within R might be capable of dealing with your
dataset.

messages.subject: Re: maximum observations in MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kristine, (cc Eric and list)

I can easily compile a version with a higher limit -- I'll do so and send to
you.  I don't want to make a larger version generally available as (1) because
MCDS is an old FORTRAN program with fixed sides arrays then having higher
maximum numbers means a bigger memory footprint, and for almost everyone 100,000
observations is enough; (2) I've made a few changes to the code that I'd like to
release in a new version of Distance soon.

If anyone else needs a version with a higher limit than 100,000 observations (or
any of the other limits) just email me.

Cheers - Len

messages.subject: Transects in a small area
messages.body_plain:
Hi
I am new to this and am hoping that someone might be able to help.
I am using Distance Sampling to estimate the density and population size =
of western ringtail possums in urban parks and remnant bush patches. Dist=
ance has been used before with this species; however, only in much larger=
 areas of bush.=20
I have my transects spaced at 40m apart, so each has an effective strip w=
idth of 20m. However, some of my parks are so small that I can only fit a=
 few transects in.=20
My questions are
1) if my transect runs along a boundry is is OK to only search for animal=
s on one side of the transect? Therefore the transect is unilateral inste=
ad of bilateral. It has been suggested to me that maybe in my analysis in=
 Distance I could half the length of the unilateral transects to deal wit=
h this. Is this correct?
2) if I want to fit a final transect in at one end can it have a smaller =
effective strip width than the other transects? For example if the bounda=
ry is approxiamtely 40m from the last transect, can I put a final transec=
t at 30m and have an effective strip width of 10m on either side for only=
 that transect. Or do all transects in the same patch that I am determini=
ng abundance need to have the same effective strip width.=20

Thankyou very much for your help! It is much appreciated
Emma

messages.body_plain:
Emma, You should also check out the meaning of "effective strip width" in the
introductory book, as it is not defined as the between-line spacing.  Instead,
it is related to the detection function: it's the distance at which as many
animals are expected to be detected beyond this distance as are expected to be
missed within it.  (Strictly, this is the effective strip half-width, but people
usually just say effective strip width, ESW.)  This is the context that Steve
was using the word in.  Cheers - Len

--

messages.subject: Covariate increases AIC (+2) but appears to improve precision of D
messages.subject_clean: Covariate increases AIC (+2) but appears to improve precision of D
messages.body_plain:
I have a couple of instances where adding a covariate increases AIC by ex=
actly 2 but gives much greater precision on D (CV~12% compared with 24% f=
rom the base model with no covariates). This result seems unlikely and I =
wonder if it could be the result of different variance calculation with M=
CDS compared with CDS. The covariate adds a single parameter which has ve=
ry poor precision.

One reason I care about this is that I want to manually model-average D. =
I would consider this covariate to be a 'pretending variable' and discard=
 this model prior to model-averaging, but the change in precision has me =
worried.

I would be grateful for any insights on why this happens and what it mean=
s.

If people would like to reply directly to wil...@landcareresearch.co.nz =
I will collate any replies and post them to the list.

Many thanks
Deb

--

messages.subject: Using the Satterthwaite method
messages.body_plain:
I have a couple of questions, but first a little background on my project:

I estimated densities of a species in seven strata (corresponding to
habitat types) using a global detection function and multiple covariates.
 I also have two habitat types that were not sampled, but for my analysis I
will assume density in each of those unsampled strata is a function of
density in one of the 7 sampled strata. To estimate the total population
size (N), I am planning on summing the seven stratum-level population
estimates plus the theorized estimates from the two unsampled strata using
the delta method (as described in section 3.7.1).  Afterwards I want to put
a confidence interval around N using the Satterthwaite adaptation described
in section 3.6.1 of the Introduction to Distance Sampling book.

Can anyone help me with these questions?

   1. How do I obtain var(n) or cv(n)?  I need one or the other to estimate
   the df in equation 3.76, which in turn is used to calculate the constant
   (the two-sided alpha-level t-distribution percentile) used in equation 3.73
   to estimate confidence intervals.  I see where the variance of sample size
   is discussed in sections 3.6.2 and 5.4, but I would like to know if it can
   be calculated in Distance rather than by hand. On page 79 there is this:
   "The calculations may be carried out in Distance by setting sample effort
   equal to ti for point i...".  In my distance project I have set sampling
   effort for points (it ranges from 4 to 1).  When I run an analysis, on the
   results page titled "Estimation Summary - Encounter rate" I see the value
   of n for each stratum, but it has no cv.  Likewise if I export the Stats
   file for the analysis, the value of n is given but it has zero as the cv.
    Have I set up my analysis incorrectly?  Or should I calculate var(n) by
   hand, or just assume var(n) = n?

   2. To obtain the equivalent of equation 3.76 for point transect
   sampling, do I just swap f(0) for h(0)?

If you are wondering why I don't just sit back and let Distance calculate
N-hat for me, there are two reasons.  First, I want to include population
estimates for the unsampled strata, and second I plan to use not just
current land area in each stratum, but also projected land area at various
times in the future, allowing me to look for change over time.

Many thanks for your help,
Chris

--

messages.subject: Animals avoiding transects... as usual
messages.body_plain:
Hi there!
I am currently helping to analyze a survey conducted along hunting
trails. I suspect animals (in our case birds) to have avoided hunting
trails and / or distances seemed to have been measured poorly /
inaccurate. I would like to inquire on any means to filter the data
(sort of a noise filtering of data to estimate the proportion of animals
missed close to the line, maybe based upon the "overloaded" next
distance bin) before we do the actual analysis. I'm cool with R,
however, I have not yet dug into the statistical analysis and
preparation of survey data outside of distance. Any suggestions on how
to improve our analysis? I attached the binning resulting from of a very
basic and quick analysis I just ran for illustration.

BTW: It is sort of annoying that the results window on my win7 pc is
half way between minimized and maximized, if you get what I mean? I've
tried to attach a screenshot that may be more congruent in its
intentions, but, as I could have expected, there isno place for image
attachments on a mailing list. I could still provide you with a
screenshot of the situation. I even drew arrows on it. :) I strongly
suspect win7 to be the problem (my personal experience with microsoft OS
rejects any other H0), but anyway, it is not that terrible (since you
just have to click on minimize, then maximize again to restore its window)!
